claims.text: Oxide-layer stability in CrFeCoNiX alloys above 900 °C is governed by the oxidation kinetics and thermodynamics of the alloying elements.
Al-containing CrFeCoNiX alloys preferentially form thermodynamically stable, slow-growing, and adherent Al2O3-containing oxide scales.
Si-containing CrFeCoNiX alloys preferentially form thermodynamically stable, slow-growing, and adherent silicate-containing oxide scales.
Al- or Si-derived oxides cooperate with chromium to produce a dense, coherent protective scale.
Mn diffuses and oxidizes faster than Al or Si in the specified CrFeCoNiX alloys.
Mn-containing alloys form comparatively porous and rapidly growing surface oxides.
The oxide scales on Mn-containing alloys are more susceptible to cracking and spallation.
Oxide phase composition and metal/oxide interfacial coherence mediate the protective behavior.
Al and Si stabilize chromia in these alloys.
Protective Al- and Si-containing oxide phases act as diffusion barriers to oxygen.
Rapid Mn oxidation creates a porous, non-coherent oxide scale.
Internal stresses cause the Mn-containing oxide scale to crack or spall.
Al- or Si-containing alloys will retain stable, coherent protective oxide layers during prolonged exposure above 900 °C.
Mn-containing alloys will exhibit unstable oxide layers, cracking or spallation, and higher oxidation rates than the Al- or Si-containing variants.
Mn-containing CrFeCoNiX serves as the baseline for comparison with Al- and Si-containing variants.
The proposed mechanism applies above 900 °C in oxidative or corrosive atmospheres.
The proposed mechanism applies to both single-phase and multiphase metallic solid-solution states.
